title: Linux Command Line Essentials
summary: Learn the Linux shell: navigating the file system, managing files, searching with pipes and redirection, permissions, processes and packages, and automating work with shell scripts. Example outputs were checked by running the commands.
audience: IT students, aspiring system administrators, developers and data analysts

lessons.title: The shell and the file system

body.p: Linux runs most of the world's servers, cloud machines, supercomputers and Android phones. On servers you usually work through a shell: a text interface where you type commands. The common shell is Bash. Learning it lets you manage servers, automate tasks and work with data quickly.

list: pwd prints the current (working) directory.
ls lists files; ls -l shows details; ls -a shows hidden files whose names start with a dot.
cd moves between directories: cd /var/log (absolute path from the root /), cd projects (relative path), cd .. (up one level), cd ~ (your home directory).
Everything starts at the root directory /. Important places include /home (users' files), /etc (configuration), /var/log (logs) and /tmp (temporary files).

body.p: Commands follow the pattern command -options arguments, for example ls -l /etc. Use man ls or ls --help to read the manual. Press Tab to complete file names and the up arrow to repeat earlier commands; both save time and typing mistakes.

body.tip: Linux is case-sensitive: Report.txt and report.txt are different files.

body.p: Most daily work is creating, copying, moving and deleting files.

list: mkdir reports creates a directory; mkdir -p a/b creates nested directories in one go.
touch notes.txt creates an empty file (or updates its timestamp).
cp file.txt backup.txt copies; cp -r folder copyfolder copies a directory.
mv old.txt new.txt renames or moves a file.
rm file.txt deletes a file; rm -r folder deletes a directory and everything in it.
Wildcards match many names: *.csv means every file ending in .csv.

body.p: There is no recycle bin in the shell: rm deletes immediately. Run ls with the same pattern first to see exactly what will be removed, and be especially careful with rm -r and wildcards.

list: cat shows a whole file; less lets you scroll (press q to quit).
head -5 file shows the first 5 lines; tail -5 the last 5; tail -f follows a growing log.
wc -l counts lines; wc -w counts words.

body.tip: Use rm -i to be asked before each deletion while you are learning.

body.p: Small commands become powerful when chained. A pipe | sends one command's output into the next. Redirection > writes output to a file (replacing it), >> appends, and < reads input from a file.
A file sales.txt has five lines: Lagos 120, Accra 80, Nairobi 95, Lagos 150, Accra 60.

list: wc -l < sales.txt prints 5, the number of lines.
grep Lagos sales.txt shows the 2 Lagos lines; grep -c Lagos counts them (2); grep -v Lagos shows lines without Lagos (3 lines).
sort -k2 -n sales.txt sorts by the second field as numbers, so head -1 then gives Accra 60, the smallest sale.
cut -d' ' -f1 sales.txt | sort | uniq -c counts each city.
awk '{s+=$2} END {print s}' sales.txt adds the second column: 505.

body.p: Redirect results to save them: grep Lagos sales.txt > lagos.txt. Find files by name with find . -name "*.log", and search inside many files with grep -r "error" /var/log.

body.tip: Build pipelines one step at a time, checking the output after each added command.

body.p: Linux is multi-user. Every file has an owner, a group and permissions for three classes: the owner (u), the group (g) and others (o). Each class can have read (r), write (w) and execute (x) permission.

ls -l shows permissions like -rwxr-xr--. The first character is the type (- for a file, d for a directory); then three sets of rwx for owner, group and others. In numeric form r = 4, w = 2, x = 1, added per class: rwx = 7, r-x = 5, r-- = 4, so chmod 754 file gives -rwxr-xr--. chmod 640 gives -rw-r-----: the owner can read and write, the group can read, others get nothing.

list: chmod u+x script.sh adds execute permission for the owner.
chown alice:staff file changes the owner and group.
sudo runs one command with administrator (root) rights, after checking you are allowed.
Avoid working as root all the time; mistakes as root can break the whole system.

body.tip: Private keys and password files should be readable only by their owner (for example chmod 600). Many tools refuse to use keys with looser permissions.

body.p: Every running program is a process with a process ID (PID). ps aux lists processes; top or htop shows live CPU and memory use; kill PID asks a process to stop, and kill -9 PID forces it.

list: Debian and Ubuntu use apt: sudo apt update refreshes the package list; sudo apt install nginx installs a web server.
Red Hat, Fedora and similar systems use dnf.
sudo apt upgrade installs security and bug-fix updates; run it regularly on servers.
systemctl status nginx shows whether a service is running.
sudo systemctl restart nginx restarts it; enable makes it start at boot.
journalctl -u nginx shows its logs; many applications also log to /var/log.
df -h shows disk space; free -h shows memory.

body.p: Remote servers are reached with SSH: ssh user@server. Use key-based login instead of passwords, and keep SSH access restricted.

body.tip: When a service fails, read its logs before changing anything; the error message usually names the problem.

body.p: A shell script is a text file of commands that runs as one program, so repetitive jobs happen the same way every time.

body.code:
#!/bin/bash
# backup.sh: copy reports into a dated folder
day=$(date +%Y-%m-%d)
mkdir -p ~/backups/$day
cp ~/reports/*.csv ~/backups/$day/
echo "Backed up $(ls ~/backups/$day | wc -l) files"

body.p: The first line (the shebang) says which program runs the script. Variables are set with name=value (no spaces) and used as $name; $( ) inserts a command's output. Make the script executable with chmod u+x backup.sh and run it with ./backup.sh.

list: if [ -f file ]; then ... fi tests whether a file exists.
for f in *.csv; do echo "$f"; done loops over files.
Quote variables ("$f") so names with spaces work.
Schedule scripts with cron: the line 0 2 * * * /home/ana/backup.sh runs it at 02:00 every day.

body.tip: Start scripts with set -e so they stop at the first failing command instead of carrying on with broken results.

quiz.q: Which command prints the current directory?
Which command creates nested directories a/b in one step?
What is the main danger of rm -r?
options: It deletes directories and their contents with no recycle bin

quiz.q: For the five-line sales.txt, what does wc -l < sales.txt print?
What does grep -c Lagos sales.txt print?
What does the pipe symbol | do?
options: Sends one command's output into the next command

quiz.q: What does > do in ls > files.txt?
options: Writes the output to files.txt, replacing its contents

quiz.q: In numeric permissions, r + w + x adds up to:

options: Runs a command with administrator rights

quiz.q: Which command installs a package on Ubuntu?
What does the cron line 0 2 * * * run?
options: On the 2nd of each month only

quiz.q: Why quote variables like "$f" in scripts?
options: So file names with spaces work correctly
